kb0_0.text: Acne is a very common skin condition that most people experience at some point. It causes spots and oily skin, and the affected skin can feel hot or painful.

kb1_0.text: Acne typically peaks in the mid-to-late teenage years and often settles by the mid-twenties, although it can persist into adulthood.

kb2_0.text: Management aims to reduce lesion severity, prevent recurrence and avoid scarring. Guideline scope covers skin-care advice, topical treatment classes, oral options and referral to specialist care for severe disease or scarring.

kb3_0.text: For mild acne, a first step is usually a topical treatment applied to the skin, and many young people find one that works; a doctor may refer to a dermatologist if needed.

kb4_0.text: Help should be sought if acne is severe or makes someone feel unwell, if scarring starts despite treatment, or if it significantly affects quality of life.

kb5_0.text: Atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis) makes skin itchy, dry, red and cracked. It is usually long-term but can improve or clear in some children as they grow.

kb6_0.text: People with atopic eczema have quieter periods and flare-ups. Triggers can include soaps, detergents, stress and the weather; it often occurs alongside asthma or hay fever.

kb7_0.text: Treatment is stepped up or down according to severity. Emollients are the foundation, with topical anti-inflammatory classes for flares; the weakest effective treatment should be used.

kb8_0.text: Painful, rapidly worsening eczema with weeping or crusting may indicate infection or eczema herpeticum and needs urgent medical review.

kb9_0.text: If eczema is severe or not improving despite treatment, a GP may refer to a specialist clinic such as dermatology.

kb10_0.text: Psoriasis is a long-lasting condition with periods of few symptoms followed by flare-ups. Triggers include skin injury, throat infections and some medicines.

kb11_0.text: The main symptom is dry, itchy, sore and flaky patches that form silvery-white scales; patches are often oval or irregular and around one to two centimetres.

kb12_0.text: Plaque psoriasis is the most common type and usually appears on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back. Generalised pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis are rare and may need emergency treatment.

kb13_0.text: Treatment usually starts with topical options; phototherapy and systemic treatments are used if topical treatment is not enough.

kb14_0.text: Some people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, an inflammatory joint condition, so recurring joint pain should be reviewed.

kb15_0.text: Melanoma may appear as a new abnormal mole, a mole that grows or changes, or a change in normal skin. Many melanomas cause no pain or itch.

metadata.source_title: Symptoms of melanoma skin cancer - Cancer Research UK

kb16_0.text: The ABCDE checklist (asymmetry, border, colour, diameter, evolution) helps flag suspicious pigmented lesions, but it is not very specific and can miss small early melanomas.

metadata.source_title: Toolbox - the ABCDE criteria for pigmented skin lesions

kb17_0.text: Normal moles are usually round or oval with a smooth edge and are typically no more than about 6 mm wide.

kb18_0.text: About half of melanomas start in normal-looking skin rather than in an existing mole.

kb19_0.text: Early melanoma is generally treated by surgical excision; if it has spread, additional treatment classes such as immunotherapy, targeted drugs or radiotherapy may be considered.

metadata.source_title: Skin cancer: the ABCDEs of melanoma

kb20_0.text: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. It grows slowly, very rarely spreads and is normally cured with treatment.

kb21_0.text: BCC may look like an open sore that does not heal, a reddish irritated patch, or a shiny red, pink or scar-like bump, usually on sun-exposed skin.

kb22_0.text: Diagnosis is sometimes clear from appearance; otherwise a small skin biopsy confirms the diagnosis and sub-type before definitive treatment.

metadata.source_title: Basal cell carcinoma - patient information leaflet (2025)

kb23_0.text: Surgery is the most common treatment for BCC; non-surgical options include photodynamic therapy and radiotherapy depending on size, site and patient factors.

metadata.source_title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) - information for patients
metadata.publisher: Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust

kb24_0.text: A skin abnormality such as a lump, ulcer or discoloured patch that has not healed after about four weeks should be checked by a GP.

metadata.source_title: Spot the signs of skin cancer

kb25_0.text: Seborrhoeic keratosis is a harmless warty spot that appears in adult life as a sign of skin ageing; some people have hundreds. Lesions look stuck on to the skin surface.

kb26_0.text: More than 90% of adults over 60 are estimated to have at least one seborrhoeic keratosis; they are uncommon before age 20.

kb27_0.text: Seborrhoeic keratosis can sometimes resemble basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma or melanoma; if doubt remains a biopsy or excision may be performed.

kb28_0.text: A seborrhoeic keratosis does not need removal, but may be removed if unsightly, itchy or catching on clothing.

kb29_0.text: SK is the most common benign epidermal tumour in dermatology practice; age, genetic predisposition and possibly UV exposure contribute.

metadata.source_title: Seborrheic keratosis (review), J Dtsch Dermatol Ges 2023;21(3):265-277

profile_Acne.text: Acne: Common condition causing spots, oily skin and sometimes painful lumps, mainly on face, chest and back. Characteristic features: oily / greasy skin, blackheads or whiteheads, red inflamed spots / pustules, painful deep lumps (nodules/cysts), lesions on face, chest or back, scarring.

profile_Eczema.text: Eczema: Atopic eczema makes skin itchy, dry, red and cracked; usually long-term with flare-ups. Characteristic features: itching, dry skin, red / inflamed patches, cracked or sore skin, flare-ups and remissions, personal/family history of asthma or hay fever, lesions in skin creases, weeping or crusted skin.

profile_Psoriasis.text: Psoriasis: Long-term condition with dry, itchy, flaky patches forming silvery-white scales; flares and remissions. Characteristic features: silvery-white scales, plaques on elbows, knees, scalp or lower back, itching, dry skin, red / inflamed patches, flare-ups and remissions, joint pain or stiffness, nail changes.

profile_Melanoma.text: Melanoma: Skin cancer of pigment cells; often first noticed as a new mole or a change in an existing mole (ABCDE). Characteristic features: new or changing mole, asymmetrical lesion, irregular border, several colours in one lesion, lesion wider than about 6 mm, bleeding or itchy lesion, brown or black lesion.

metadata.source_title: Symptoms of melanoma skin cancer - Cancer Research UK

profile_Basal Cell Carcinoma.text: Basal Cell Carcinoma: Most common, slow-growing skin cancer; usually a pearly bump or non-healing sore on sun-exposed skin. Characteristic features: shiny / pearly bump, sore that does not heal, on a sun-exposed site (face, ears, neck), slowly growing lesion, bleeding or itchy lesion.

profile_Seborrheic Keratosis.text: Seborrheic Keratosis: Very common harmless 'stuck-on' warty growth of adult skin; dark ones can resemble melanoma. Characteristic features: 'stuck-on' waxy lesion, brown or black lesion, rough, warty surface, older adult (typically 50+), multiple similar lesions, itching.

profile_Skin Cancer (unspecified).text: Skin Cancer (unspecified): Dataset umbrella label for malignant skin lesions without sub-type (melanoma, BCC, SCC, ...). Characteristic features: new or changing mole, sore that does not heal, bleeding or itchy lesion, slowly growing lesion, brown or black lesion, shiny / pearly bump.
